In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new materials, and the evaluation of existing materials for use in protective clothing.
the development of a new instrument for measuring bacterial transfer through fabrics used for the protection of burn patients.
the design of barrier garments for use in the nursing of burns.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
barrier garments should not be made of plastic or waterproofed cotton at points of skin-to-skin contact where the garment is likely to become wet with wound secretions.
a fabric that is waterproof and has a low wettabiity will be a good barrier to bacteria.
barrier garments should have a high water resistance, a high water repellency, and a low wettibility, but should also be permeable to water vapour.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the penetration of bacteria through fabrics designed for use as barrier clothing can be predicted by the water permeability of the fabric and the wettability of its outer surface.
the penetration of bacteria through barrier clothing depends on the wetting of the clothing, and not on the water repellency of the clothing.

a barrier garment should be made of either plastic or of recently water proofed, closely woven cotton at those points of contact between the nurse and patient where there is a likelihood that the clothes may become wetted by bacteria containing wound exudates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
barrier clothing is an essential component of a burn patient care system, and it should be used as part of a comprehensive burn care plan.
the use of barrier fabrics is not sufficient to prevent the spread of bacteria from patients to nurses and from nurses to patients, and that other measures are needed to protect both parties.

barrier fabrics should have low wettability, and that barrier garments should not be laundered more than 10 times, as this increases the wettability of the fabrics and increases the transfer of bacteria.
